'''''Solanum aethiopicum''''', the '''bitter tomato''', '''Ethiopian eggplant''',<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.flowersofindia.net/catalog/slides/Bitter%20Tomato.html|title=Solanum aethiopicum - Bitter Tomato|website=www.flowersofindia.net|access-date=2017-12-18}}</ref> or '''nakati''', is a fruiting [[plant]] of the [[genus]] ''[[Solanum]]'' mainly found in [[Asia]] and Tropical [[Africa]]. It is also known as '''Ethiopian nightshade''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SOAE2|taxon=Solanum aetiopicum|accessdate=16 November 2015}}</ref> '''garden eggs, pumpkin-on-a-stick''',<ref>{{Cite web |title=Capsicum 'Pumpkin on a Stick' |url=https://cutflowers.ces.ncsu.edu/capsicum-pumpkin-on-a-stick/ |access-date=2022-09-17 |website=cutflowers.ces.ncsu.edu |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Pumpkin-on-a-stick |url=https://blogs.cornell.edu/hightunnels/flowers/cut-flowers/cut-flower-crops/pumpkin-on-a-stick/ |access-date=2022-09-17 |website=blogs.cornell.edu}}</ref> and '''mock tomato'''. It is a popular vegetable in north-east India, and is known as '''khamen akhaba''' in Manipuri and ''samṭawk'' in [[Mizo language|Mizo]]. They are called ''Titay bii'' or simply ''bii'' in Darjeeling, Sikkim and Nepal, and are relished with meat, particularly pork. These names are a result of its varied morphology, with ripe fruit often looking like a cross between an [[eggplant]] and a [[tomato]], which are also from ''Solanum''. In fact, the Ethiopian eggplant was so much confused with the ordinary eggplant that this was considered by some a [[variety (botany)|variety]] ''violaceum'' of  ''S. aethiopicum''.

== Genetics ==
Ethiopian eggplant may have originated from the domestication of  ''[[Solanum anguivi]]''. The [[scarlet eggplant]], also known as Gilo or ''jiló'', was long held to be a distinct species (''S. gilo'') but is nowadays generally considered to be a [[cultivar]] group of ''S. aethiopicum''.

==Uses==
The leaves of ''Solanum aethiopicum'' are eaten as a [[leaf vegetable]] and are actually more nutritious than the [[fruit]].

The highly variable fruit of the plant is eaten both raw and cooked and is becoming more popular as a cultivated crop. These fruits are usually harvested while still green, before the skin becomes thick. Bitterness increases with higher levels of [[saponin]] in the fruit, some varieties being sweet and others very bitter. When the berries mature, they turn bright red because of high [[carotene]] content.

''Solanum aethiopicum'' is used as an ornamental in Asia.

In Nigeria, Igbo people use it as a substitute for [[kola nut]], especially for those who do not want to chew kola nut, in  which case it is used to welcome guests at home or before resumption of a traditional ceremony.

Garden egg, as it is commonly known in Nigeria, is sometimes used to make a tomato-based sauce which can be used to eat yam.

===Cultivation===
[[Image:Solanum aethiopicum MS 2264.JPG|thumb|Fruit of ''S. aethiopicum'' from SW Burkina Faso]]

Currently there is a large movement towards increased cultivation of ''Solanum aethiopicum'' in West Africa. It grows all year long and can produce high fruit yields. However, low germination rates are an obstacle to wider cultivation.

[[Image:Melanzana rossa di Rotonda.jpg|thumb|Melanzana rossa di [[Rotonda, Basilicata]], variety of ''S. aethiopicum'' cultivated in Italy]]

The only place where ''S. aethiopicum'' is grown to a significant extent in Europe lies in South Italy, in [[Rotonda, Basilicata|Rotonda]] in the [[Basilicata]], where this plant is of some commercial importance. It was likely introduced by veterans returning from East Africa after the colonial war in the late 19th century.

[[Image:Chicken-Bitter-Tomato.jpg|thumb|Chicken cooked with bitter tomato in northeast India]]

===Cultivars===
Cultivars have been allocated into four groups, termed Gilo, Shum, Kumba and Aculeatum.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lester |first1=R.N. |title=Taxonomy of Scarlet Eggplants, Solanum Aethiopicum L |journal=Acta Horticulturae |date=July 1986 |issue=182 |pages=125–132 |doi=10.17660/ActaHortic.1986.182.15}}</ref> Gilo are grown only for fruit, Shum only for their leaves, Kumba are grown for both their leaves and fruit, Aculateum are ornamental.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nakyewa |first1=Brenda |last2=Sseremba |first2=Godfrey |last3=Kabod |first3=Nahamya Pamela |last4=Rwothtimutung |first4=Moses |last5=Kyebalyenda |first5=Tadeo |last6=Waholi |first6=Kenneth |last7=Buteme |first7=Ruth |last8=Nakanwangi |first8=Mildred Julian |last9=Bishop |first9=Gerard |last10=Kizito |first10=Elizabeth Balyejusa |title=Farmer preferred traits and genotype choices in Solanum aethiopicum L., Shum group |journal=Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine |date=13 April 2021 |volume=17 |issue=1 |pages=27 |doi=10.1186/s13002-021-00455-y |pmid=33849577 |pmc=8042716 |doi-access=free |issn=1746-4269}}</ref>

* ''''Turkish Orange'''' or ''''Turkish Italian''''
: The fruits of this variety are about 2 inches in diameter and turn bright orange-red when ripe, although they are usually eaten when still green. The sweet taste is often used in [[Thai curry]]. It can produce fruit within just 75 days after planting.
:
* ''''Sweet Red''''
: These striped fruits, just 1 inch in diameter, have a strong but non-bitter flavor. The plant is thornless and grows up to 3 feet tall. It can produce fruit 125 days after planting.
:
* ''''Small Ruffled Red'''', ''''Red Ruffles'''', or ''''Hmong Red''''
: The two-inch berries of the 'Hmong Red' have deep creases and a bitter flavor used in Southeast Asian cooking. It can produce fruit 100 days after planting.
:
* ''''[[Scarlet eggplant|Gilo]]'''', ''''[[Scarlet eggplant|Jiló]]'''', ''''[[Scarlet eggplant]]'''' or '''garden eggs'''
: Grown mainly in [[Brazil]] and sub-Saharan Africa.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Mangan |first1=Frank |last2=Barros |first2=Zoraia |last3=Marchese |first3=Aline |last4=Godoy-Hernández |first4=Heriberto |title=Garden Egg |url=https://worldcrops.org/crops/garden-egg/index.html |website=worldcrops.org |access-date=5 August 2025}}</ref> It has a bitter taste and is usually consumed cooked. The plant takes 75 days to reach maturity. Plants vary in size, shape, taste, etc.
:
*''''Liberian eggplant'''' 
: Landrace from [[Liberia]]. Immature fruit are white in color. They are used in soups and stews like Tabughee. The plant takes 85 days to reach maturity.
